what_it_does: Modern chips increasingly combine a general-purpose processor with a programmable logic chip called an FPGA (field-programmable gate array — a chip whose circuits can be reconfigured in software) on the same piece of silicon, forming a heterogeneous system-on-chip. The processor side has a well-established security feature called TrustZone, which creates a walled-off secure area where sensitive code (like encryption keys or authentication logic) can run without being visible to the rest of the system. The problem is that TrustZone only protects the processor, not the FPGA fabric sitting next to it, so workloads that run on the FPGA side are left unprotected. This paper introduces FPGA-TrustZone, which extends the same isolation guarantees to the FPGA by enforcing access controls at the interconnect (the on-chip bus that connects the processor and FPGA) and inside the FPGA fabric itself. The goal is to let trusted and untrusted FPGA code coexist safely on the same chip, mirroring the guarantees that TrustZone already provides for processor code.
